judged.justification: Frames Dionysius as Proclean in a discussion of the Oration's own mystical sources.
Reverses the received individualist reading of the Oration.

quotes.t: The Oration has said nothing yet about Kabbalah when the orator announces that “with their more secret theology, Hebrews too sometimes
transform the blessed Enoch into an angel of divinity, whom they call מטטרון”—Metatron.
But the Oration, supplying none of this context, introduces the angel and a “more secret theology” with hints about Kabbalah entirely beyond the grasp of Christians.

judged.justification: Explains the Metatron reference as a deliberately concealed Kabbalistic signal.
States the Metatron-Pallas equation of 2K10 in Copenhaver's translation.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes Abulafia in a text translated for Pico.

judged.justification: Reads the angelic life as a soteriological aspiration for fallen humans.
Ties the three orders to the Dionysian triad and to the Zohar's angelic leaders.
Establishes the Dionysian, not Hebrew, provenance of the Thrones.
States the tripartite scheme (agency, psychology, substance) in one place.
Shows Pico's Thrones-as-judgment departs from Dionysius and follows Psalm and Gregory.

quotes.t: The Areopagite’s nine ranks became canonical for Christians, though Jewish tradition often preferred ten groups. In a Kabbalist text known to Pico, the names were those that he used in the Conclusions, while changing the order:
There are nine hierarchies of angels, whose names are Cherubim, Seraphim, Hasmalim, Haiot, Aralim, Tarsisim, Ophanim, Thephsarim, and Isim.

judged.justification: Keeps the Hebrew nine hierarchies distinct from Dionysius' nine.

quotes.t: T1K30 No angel with six wings ever changes. The immutable angels were Seraphim and Cherubim, but Pico mentioned Cherubim first, ready for humans to emulate in a “Cherubic life,” whereas Seraphs blazed beyond reach and Thrones reached down toward “lower …

judged.justification: Equates the Kabbalistic Hasmalim with the Dionysian Thrones.
Gives Copenhaver's summary of the ascent in the order judging, knowing, loving.

quotes.t: The Cherub is the “knot” that ties these “primary minds” together, said Pico. Pallas, goddess of wisdom and “protector of contemplative philosophy,” governs this angelic order. Since thesis T2K10 identifies “what Orpheus names Pallas” as Metatron—within the Seraphic fire surrounding …

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers the Pallas-Metatron-Wisdom identification from thesis T2K10 and the location of Metatron within the Seraphic fire.

open.t: Copenhaver locates Metatron within the Seraphic fire yet has Pallas govern the Cherubic order; the passage does not explain how the two placements fit.

judged.justification: Reads the Order of Pallas passage as Kabbalistic: the Cherub governed by Pallas is Metatron and S2.

quotes.t: Pico, who could see Pallas in this Kabbalist way, also learned mysteries from Proclus, from other pagan Platonists and from Ficino, their master explicator.
Although Pallas actually had no role in the Chaldean theology, Proclus replaced her with Hecate, also well-armed and philosophy’s protector in the Oracles.

bears.note: Ficino, as master explicator of pagan Platonists, is a channel for Pico's Pallas material.
Ficino mediates Proclus to Pico; Copenhaver calls him Pico's friend.

warrants.t: An inference from Ficino's letter to Lorenzo about Pico's arrival and the later ten-year gap.

bears.note: Copenhaver characterizes Pico as arrogant and careless even with friends, and infers earlier friction with Ficino.

judged.justification: Adds a hint of friction beneath Ficino's celebratory account of the meeting.

bears.note: Contrasts Ficino's explicatory practice with Pico's deliberate mystification.

judged.justification: Sets Ficino's method against Pico's for the same Platonic material.
Makes the Cherubic life, not the Seraphic, the practical model.
Ties the Kabbalistic thesis to Dionysian apophatic theology.

quotes.t: At the top of the angelic hierarchy, as described by Dionysius, were Thrones to cleanse sinners, Cherubs to enlighten them, and Seraphs to perfect them.

judged.justification: Places the Cherubic light below the final mystical dissolution.
Presents Dionysius as a theurgic Neoplatonist in the setting of the Oration.

quotes.t: More useful to Pico, perhaps, was a Book of Imaginary Circles by Ibn al-Sid al-Batalyawsi, known to Jews in the prince’s Italy. Convinced that higher realities transcend ordinary geometry, Batalyawsi envisioned a straight line or ladder running between two circles …

open.t: Whether Pico used Batalyawsi is left open by the word 'perhaps'.

judged.justification: Reads the Job passage as Kabbalistic angelology (Michael and Gabriel) not only ethics.
Links the two archangels to sefirotic positions.
Ties the Job peace to angel magic and Metatron.
Names the three sources of the Oration's mysticism in one sentence.

open.t: The quotation about the mid-day light is cited to a source in Copenhaver's note 43 (not read here); it is not clear from the passage alone whether the words are Augustine's or Pico's paraphrase.

judged.justification: Maps the three archangels onto the curriculum and the Sefirot.

quotes.t: The very first of Pico’s Kabbalist theses (T1K1) introduces Michael, stationed below these loftier spirits but a high priest nonetheless. The purpose of his priesthood is for saints to be sacrificed by a good death of the kiss.

Souls to be saved must rise through the place where Abraham presides and where Michael “sacrifices the souls of the just.” In theosophical space, the place is S4, just beneath the supreme triad where annihilation in the Godhead waits.

judged.justification: Places Michael's priesthood at S4.
Presents Michael as a benign messenger of death and the giver of the priesthood of theology.

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers what Ficino and Poliziano knew; no direct evidence is quoted at this point.

bears.note: Copenhaver has Ficino know only 'more or less' what Pico was doing.
Copenhaver has Poliziano know only 'more or less' what Pico was doing.
Flavius and other Jews helped Pico with Kabbalah and understood his project best.

copenhaver2019-angels:049.hedge_words: will have known what their friend was up to, more or less

judged.justification: Assigns Flavius, not Ficino, the best understanding of the Kabbalistic project.

open.t: Whether Pico deliberately concealed angel-magic while advertising natural magic is posed as a question, answered only that the magic theses 'suggest so'.

judged.justification: Proposes that the Oration's natural magic conceals an angel-magic visible only in the Kabbalistic theses.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes Abulafia on the Agent Intellect and its names.

judged.justification: Links the Cherub, Enoch and Metatron with the Agent Intellect.

bears.note: Copenhaver contrasts Pico's route to supernatural magic through Kabbalah with Ficino's use of occult qualities.

judged.justification: States what the Oration does not say about angels in its defence of magic.

quotes.t: He wanted them to “turn into separate angels” by attaining the state of prophecy and to be “saved by this from natural death on the day of their . . . death and live forever.”
including rites to join with Metatron, the angel prince identified by Abulafia with the Agent Intellect.

Mystical union with the Intellect or Metatron eradicates the self. In Abulafia’s conception, however, the self vanishes not only within the Mind but also in favor of others because the mystic’s role is messianic as well as prophetic.

judged.justification: Connects Abulafian union with the Intellect to the Oration's angelic transformation.

open.t: Whether Pico actually learned that Metatron is the Messiah, El Shaddai and the Shekinah is posed only as a condition.

judged.justification: Connects Metatron with the Christian Trinity via Shaddai and the Shekinah.

bears.note: The passage explains why Pico's angel-magic could be seen as dangerous for a Christian.

open.t: What the Oration means by a finished metaphysics of angelic forms is left open by Copenhaver.

judged.justification: Grounds Pico's derivation of the Trinity in Proclean triads.

bears.note: Pico asked to borrow Ficino's copy of Iamblichus.

judged.justification: Places Pico's angel theses in the ordinary scholastic curriculum rather than magic.

open.t: Whether Pico knew Abu Ma'shar's identification of Idris with Enoch and Hermes is left open.

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers a possible link between Flavius's history with Cibò and the pope's view of Pico.

bears.note: Copenhaver offers Flavius's earlier friction with Cibò as a possible factor in Innocent VIII's judgment of Pico.
Flavius had alienated Cibò before Cibò was pope.
Background to the condemnation of thirteen theses.

judged.justification: Offers a personal rather than doctrinal factor in the condemnation.

bears.note: On this reading the Oration's angelic message was undetectable by the intended Christian audience.

judged.justification: Puts the change into angels, by magic and Kabbalah, at the centre of the Oration.
Reads the Oration as an exhortation to angel magic.
Reverses the reading of dignitas as human dignity: it is an angelic rank.
Characterizes the Cherubic life as bodiless and sexless.
States what the Oration does and does not show of Kabbalah.

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes the Asclepius on animating idols with the souls of demons or angels.

judged.justification: Explains Pico's silence about Hermetic angel-and-demon idol magic.
Frames the Sefirot as actors, not angels.
Angels are fixed in nature while humans can become angels.
The Oration's only mention of Metatron by name comes in a list of metamorphoses.
The three orders correspond to love, intelligence, judgment.
The ordering judging-knowing-loving is not the Dionysian order.
The Order of Pallas is named here, not glossed; the gloss is in T2K10.
The Oration says only that Kabbalah teaches 'the orders of angels' in agreement with Dionysius.
States the nine Hebrew hierarchies in Pico's own thesis, kept distinct from Dionysian nine.
Pico's own wording of the Metatron-Pallas equation.
Places angel and rational soul on a scale beneath a God who is not an intellect.

quotes.t: In T2K10, a space to be filled by a Hebrew word is blank in the printed edition of the Conclusions; Ebgi 2014, 215–225, prefers Hokmah, S2, following a commentary by Francesco Zorzi; Wirszubski’s choice of Metatron seems better, however, because …

warrants.t: Copenhaver argues from the match with the other entities named in the thesis and from another thesis that identifies the Agent Intellect with Metatron.

open.t: Which Hebrew word stood in the blank of T2K10 (Metatron or Hokmah) is disputed; Ebgi and Wirszubski differ.

judged.justification: Records that the Metatron reading of 2K10 is an editorial restoration, not a printed word.

open.t: The glossary calls the knot of primary minds 'the highest angels' whereas the chapter has the Cherub tie the knot; the two are not reconciled in the glossary.

judged.justification: Glossary summary of the Pallas-Metatron identification.
Dates the angel-and-demon hierarchy of Platonism after Plotinus.
